brief-1.text: Peak seats are perishable, sold-out inventory, unlike gym floor space. Friday and Saturday evenings sold out on 80% of dates, so every member admission on those nights displaces a roughly €34 sale, whereas an extra gym member at peak only adds crowding. A strong reply flags this and limits, caps or blacks out member bookings on high-demand performances (for example steering members toward Tuesday to Thursday, which averaged 49%).

The licensing terms break the flat-fee model. Member admissions carry no price at the point of booking, so they would almost certainly count as complimentary (issued at under half face value), and complimentary admissions are capped at 4% of the house, about 20 of 520 seats per performance. Gyms and streaming services pay no per-admission royalties. A strong reply catches the cap and its consequence: members can be seated in only about 20 seats a performance unless rights holders agree new terms or member admissions are assigned a value for royalty purposes.

A gym visit reserves nothing; a theatre booking reserves a perishable seat. With zero cost per booking, members can book speculatively and not turn up, and the 14% no-show rate on complimentary tickets (versus 3% on paid) shows what free admissions do here. On sell-out nights each no-show is an empty seat that could have been sold. A strong reply flags this and proposes a control such as a no-show penalty, booking limits or releasing unclaimed member seats.

Gym economics depend on breakage: many payers who rarely come. Here the likeliest buyers are existing heavy attenders. The 1,100 subscribers already pay €182 a year for seven shows and would pay €180 a year for unlimited access; the 1,800 frequent attenders who buy a third of single tickets spend at least about €136 a year each; occasional attenders gain little from a €180-a-year commitment. A strong reply sees that the pass mostly re-prices the existing core audience downward (cannibalization) rather than adding paying-but-absent members.

brief-2.text: Fire spreads contiguously through adjacent fuel, so a narrow break stops it. This disease jumps: its beetle vector flies up to 3 km, so a 400 m ring cannot contain spread. A strong reply says the firebreak geometry does not match the spread mechanism.

A fire front is visible; this front is not. Symptoms appear 18 to 24 months after infection, and 6 of 20 symptom-free trees sampled just outside the visible patch were already infected, so a ring drawn around visible symptoms sits inside the real front. A strong reply catches the latency and calls for mapping the outbreak by sampling and surveillance beyond the visible patch before deciding where any boundary goes.

Cutting a firebreak removes fuel; cutting here creates it. The beetle breeds in freshly cut or dying beech, and felled timber normally sits stacked at the roadside until late summer, through the whole May to July flight season. Winter clear-felling of a 400 m ring would put a large mass of breeding material next to the outbreak and could amplify the vector. A strong reply flags this and requires felled material to be removed, chipped, debarked or otherwise dealt with before May, or argues against felling healthy trees at all.

Fires are not carried off in car boots; this disease can be. Tallis Ford sells firewood cut from the surrounding woods to about 9,000 campers a summer, and many take leftover logs home, which can seed distant outbreaks no perimeter can stop. A strong reply flags firewood movement as a long-distance spread route and calls for stopping or controlling it.

brief-3.text: A sick club works because illness strikes members independently, so the well majority pays for the unlucky few. Slow months here are shared and predictable: 31 of 46 members had their two lowest months in January and August, so many participants would claim in the same months every year. A strong reply sees that this is predictable, correlated seasonal variation rather than an independent, insurable risk, that the pool faces concentrated recurring drains, and proposes something like individual smoothing reserves or a seasonally adjusted trigger instead of pure pooling.

Illness is certified by someone outside the fund and is not chosen; the proposed trigger is neither. Members invoice their own clients, so they control which month income lands in, and they can decline desk offers without penalty. A member can push a month below 60% of their average by delaying invoices or turning down work, collect a top-up, then invoice the following month. A strong reply identifies this specific manipulability of the trigger and proposes one members cannot easily move (for example income measured over several months, or counting declined offers).

A sick club bridges a temporary interruption followed by recovery. The Halcyra change is a lasting structural shift in about half the co-op's work by value, toward lower-paid post-editing of machine drafts. A smoothing fund cannot finance a permanent decline: it would pay out across many members at once while their trailing averages fall, then stop helping as the 60% threshold ratchets down. A strong reply separates this from the fund design and says it needs a different response (pricing, retraining, diversifying clients), not the pool.

Dockers could not see illness coming; freelancers can see their own pipelines (a client winding down, a contract ending). With joining voluntary and open at any time, members can enrol just before a known dry spell and stay out while busy. A strong reply flags this adverse selection and proposes a fix such as a waiting period, a minimum membership term or automatic membership.
